title: Bengali Medical Interpretation: Dialect and Workflow Guide
summary: Build a Bengali medical interpretation workflow for language variety, spoken and written preferences, and clear understanding.
body_markdown:
###


Yes. Bengali and Bangla refer to the same language, but a United States healthcare record should still capture the patient’s own language label and any regional variety they report. The record should also keep spoken-language preference separate from written-language and script preference.


###


Yes, when the healthcare organization serves patients who identify Sylheti as their preferred spoken language or variety. In a United States intake workflow, allow self-identification, keep the patient’s wording, and confirm the preferred language at the encounter instead of inferring it from country, ethnicity, surname, or family language.


###


No. Spoken-language preference does not establish written-language preference or reading comfort. In a clinical discharge workflow, ask whether the patient wants Bengali, English, bilingual material, another language, or a spoken review, and use teach-back to confirm understanding.


###


Clinicians should confirm the medication name, strength, dose, route, timing, duration, and conditional instructions through interpretation, then ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words. In United States care settings, this teach-back step checks whether the explanation was clear; it does not replace medication reconciliation or clinical review.


###


AI interpretation with defined quality controls can be a first-line option for Bengali encounters when the organization has tested the intended language variety, clinical use case, audio conditions, and escalation path. A complementary human interpreter can be used according to patient preference, organizational policy, and encounter needs.
